You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF at S1).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.2 V at S1; compare it with the
output window and the diode drops.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: low frequency, mid load; Ip = 25 uA peak, f = 50 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 680 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: high frequency, small Cp, light load; Ip = 100 uA peak, f = 200 Hz, Cp = 17.5 nF, RL = 4700 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: low frequency, large Cp; Ip = 25 uA peak, f = 50 Hz, Cp = 32.5 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: high frequency, large Cp, heavy load; Ip = 100 uA peak, f = 200 Hz, Cp = 32.5 nF, RL = 150 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: hot, heavy load; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 200 kOhm, temperature 85 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:

S2       2.04    2.09    83.1   0.518      6.14  ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL     FAIL    
S3        4.2    4.21    23.2  0.0865      3.75  ok       FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL    
S4       1.79    1.82    57.1   0.759      3.21  FAIL     ok       FAIL     FAIL     FAIL    
S5       1.74    1.74    8.96       -      20.1  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S6       1.55    1.56    25.4       -        12  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:

 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",

    },
    {

      "pzp",

     ],

    },
    {
     "id": "S1",

     "nodes": [
      "n1",

     ],

    },
    {

    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

reply.reasoning:
*   Goal: $V_{out,min} \ge 1.8\text{V}$, $V_{out,max} \le 3.6\text{V}$, $V_{pp} \le 0.05\text{V}$, $t_{up} \le 0.4\text{s}$, $dV \le 0.02\text{V}$.
    *   Piezo: $I_p \sin(2\pi ft)$, $C_p$ (25nF nominal), 20M$\Omega$ leakage.
    *   $V_{oc,peak} = I_p / (2\pi f C_p)$.
        *   S1: $50\mu\text{A} / (2\pi \cdot 100 \cdot 25\text{nF}) \approx 3.18\text{V}$.
        *   S2: $25\mu\text{A} / (2\pi \cdot 50 \cdot 25\text{nF}) \approx 3.18\text{V}$.
        *   S3: $100\mu\text{A} / (2\pi \cdot 200 \cdot 17.5\text{nF}) \approx 4.54\text{V}$.
        *   S4: $25\mu\text{A} / (2\pi \cdot 50 \cdot 32.5\text{nF}) \approx 2.45\text{V}$.
        *   S5: $100\mu\text{A} / (2\pi \cdot 200 \cdot 32.5\text{nF}) \approx 2.45\text{V}$.
        *   S6: $50\mu\text{A} / (2\pi \cdot 100 \cdot 25\text{nF}) \approx 3.18\text{V}$.

        *   S4 settled: $dV = 0.066\text{V}$ (too slow).
        *   S4 ripple: $V_{pp} = 0.069\text{V}$ (too high).
        *   Wait, S4 passed everything else. This is *very* close. The issue is the time constant and the ripple.
        *   Increasing $C_{out}$ usually reduces ripple but increases startup time ($t_{up}$) and settlement time ($dV$).
        *   Wait, the `PSSHI_Zener` uses a full bridge (D1-D4) AND an inductor (L1) with a switch (S1) for SSHI.
        *   Wait, looking at the topology of `PSSHI_Zener` (c0068):
            L1: pzp -> n1
            S1: n1 -> pzn (ctrl G1)
            D1: pzp -> out
            D2: pzn -> out
            D3: 0 -> pzp
            D4: 0 -> pzn
            D5: 0 -> out (DZ33)
            C1: out -> 0
            This is a Parallel-SSHI (PSSHI) structure. The L-S1 branch is in parallel with the piezo, acting as an inverter to flip the charge.

        *   S2 ripple: $0.060\text{V}$ (too high).
        *   S6 ripple: $0.064\text{V}$ (too high).
        *   This topology uses synchronous switches instead of diodes.

        *   S5, S6: $V_{out,min} < 1.8\text{V}$ (insufficient power).
        *   S2 settled: $dV > 0.02\text{V}$.

    *   `PSSHI_Zener` is the strongest. It fails on S4's ripple and settlement.
    *   S4 has low frequency (50Hz), large $C_p$ (32.5nF), and a mid-load (1M$\Omega$).
    *   $V_{oc,peak}$ for S4 is only 2.45V. This explains why it's struggle. The PSSHI helps by increasing the effective voltage.
    *   If $dV$ is too high, the system hasn't reached steady state. This means the charging current is very small compared to the storage capacitor $C_1$.
    *   If $V_{pp}$ is too high, the storage capacitor $C_1$ is too small to buffer the pulse.
    *   This is a contradiction: $C_1$ too small (ripple) vs $C_1$ too large (settlement). However, for S4, $V_{pp}$ is 69mV (limit 50mV) and $dV$ is 67mV (limit 20mV).
    *   Wait, $dV$ is $|mean(0.7-0.8) - mean(0.6-0.7)|$. If $dV$ is large, it means the output is still climbing.
    *   If we increase $C_{out}$ to fix ripple, $dV$ will get *worse* because it will take longer to charge.
    *   If we decrease $C_{out}$ to fix $dV$, ripple will get *worse*.
    *   The only way to fix both is to increase the *average power* delivered to the load.

    *   The `PSSHI_Zener` has an inductor L1 and a switch S1. It's effectively flipping the piezo voltage.
    *   Maybe a more efficient SSHI or a different inverter could help.
    *   What about a SEH (Synchronized Electric Harvesting) or SSHI (Synchronized Switch Harvesting on Inductor) with a more optimized bridge?
    *   The `PSSHI_Zener` uses a full bridge (D1-D4). This introduces 2 diode drops (~0.5V) per cycle.
    *   If we use synchronous switches for the rectification part as well, we eliminate those drops.
    *   Wait, `SyncBridge_Zener` (c0021) already did that. It passed S4 but failed ripple on S2/S6.
    *   Can we combine the Inductor-Switch (SSHI) with the Synchronous Bridge?
    *   Let's try a "Sync-SSHI" topology:
        *   An inductor-switch for charge inversion (to boost power).
        *   A synchronous bridge for rectification (to remove diode drops).
    *   Wait, the `SyncBridge_Zener` (c0021) is:
        S1: pzp -> out, S2: pzn -> out, S3: 0 -> pzn, S4: 0 -> pzp.
        This is a full bridge of switches.
        If we add an inductor-switch (L1, S_inv) in parallel with the piezo, we get SSHI + Synchronous Bridge.

    *   Proposed Structure: SSHI + Sync-Bridge
        - L1: pzp -> n1
        - S_inv: n1 -> pzn (ctrl G_inv)
        - S1: pzp -> out (ctrl G1)
        - S2: pzn -> out (ctrl G2)
        - S3: 0 -> pzn (ctrl G1)
        - S4: 0 -> pzp (ctrl G2)
        - G_inv: SYNC (edges: both, ton=...)
        - G1: SYNC (edges: pos, ton=...)
        - G2: SYNC (edges: neg, ton=...)
        - D_zener: 0 -> out (DZ33)
        - C_out: out -> 0

    *   Wait, I only have 4 switches maximum.
        - S1, S2, S3, S4 (Sync bridge) = 4 switches.
        - S_inv = 1 switch.
        - Total = 5 switches. (Too many).

    *   Okay, if I can't have a full sync bridge and an inverter, I must choose.
    *   `PSSHI_Zener` used: 1 switch (S1) + 4 diodes (D1-D4). Total = 5 components for the power path.
    *   `SyncBridge_Zener` used: 4 switches.
    *   Could we use a half-bridge?
        - Piezo pzp, pzn.
        - Sync switch S1: pzp -> out.
        - Sync switch S2: pzn -> out.
        - Diodes for the return path: D1: 0 -> pzp, D2: 0 -> pzn.
        - This uses 2 switches and 2 diodes.
        - Now I have 2 switches left for an inverter (L1, S_inv).
        - S_inv: n1 -> pzn (ctrl G_inv).
        - Total switches: 3. Total diodes: 2. Total inductors: 1. (Within limits).

    *   Wait, is there a better way to do the inversion?
        What if we use the `SyncBridge` but replace two of the switches with diodes?
        No, the `SyncBridge` already performs rectification. The PSSHI part (L1, S_inv) is what boosts the power.

    *   Let's refine the "Sync-Half-Bridge + PSSHI":
        L1: pzp -> n1
        S_inv: n1 -> pzn (ctrl G_inv, edges: both)
        S1: pzp -> out (ctrl G1, edges: pos)
        S2: pzn -> out (ctrl G2, edges: neg)
        D1: 0 -> pzp (DSCH)
        D2: 0 -> pzn (DSCH)
        D_zener: 0 -> out (DZ33)
        C_out: out -> 0

    *   Will this work?
        - When $V_{pzp}$ is positive (peak), G1 closes S1, and D2 conducts. Current flows $pzp \rightarrow out \rightarrow 0 \rightarrow pzn$.
        - When $V_{pzn}$ is positive (peak), G2 closes S2, and D1 conducts. Current flows $pzn \rightarrow out \rightarrow 0 \rightarrow pzp$.
        - Inversion: G_inv closes S_inv at the peaks to flip the voltage.

    *   Wait, let's look at `PSSHI_Zener` again. It used a full diode bridge.
        If we just replace the two diodes that connect to `out` with switches, we reduce the voltage drop.
        - D1: pzp -> out (Replace with S1, ctrl G1, edges: pos)
        - D2: pzn -> out (Replace with S2, ctrl G2, edges: neg)
        - D3: 0 -> pzp (Keep as diode)
        - D4: 0 -> pzn (Keep as diode)
        - L1: pzp -> n1
        - S_inv: n1 -> pzn (ctrl G_inv, edges: both)
        - This uses 3 switches (S1, S2, S_inv) and 2 diodes (D3, D4). Total 5.

    *   Wait, the "S4 settled" and "S4 ripple" in `PSSHI_Zener` are very small failures.
        $V_{pp} = 69\text{mV}$ (vs $50\text{mV}$) and $dV = 67\text{mV}$ (vs $20\text{mV}$).
        If we increase the power delivered, we can increase $C_{out}$ to fix ripple without hurting $dV$ too much.
        Reducing the diode drop from 2 diodes to 1 diode (on the `out` path) should increase the voltage and the current delivered to $C_{out}$.

    *   Wait, let's think about the `S4` case specifically. $V_{oc,peak}$ is 2.45V.
        With a full bridge of DSCH, you lose $2 \times 0.25\text{V} = 0.5\text{V}$.
        $V_{out}$ will be around $2.45 - 0.5 = 1.95\text{V}$ (roughly).
        If we replace two diodes with switches, we only lose 1 diode drop ($0.25\text{V}$).
        $V_{out}$ will be around $2.45 - 0.25 = 2.2\text{V}$.
        This increase in voltage and power should help a lot with the settlement time $dV$ and allow for a larger $C_{out}$ to reduce ripple.

    *   Let's call this `PSSHI_SyncHalf`.
        - L1: pzp -> n1
        - S1: n1 -> pzn (ctrl G_inv, edges: both)
        - S2: pzp -> out (ctrl G1, edges: pos)
        - S3: pzn -> out (ctrl G2, edges: neg)
        - D1: 0 -> pzp (DSCH)
        - D2: 0 -> pzn (DSCH)
        - D3: 0 -> out (DZ33)
        - C1: out -> 0

    *   Is there any other topology?
        Maybe a "Synchronous SSHI" where the inverter is part of the bridge? (Too complex).
        What about a simpler SSHI without the Zener, but with a different $C_{out}$? No, the Zener is needed for $V_{out,max}$ on S3.

    *   Let's try to optimize the `PSSHI_SyncHalf` and maybe one other variation.
        Variation 2: Full Sync Bridge + InductorInverter? (Already said 5 switches, too many).
        Variation 3: Use a single SYNC to control both rectification and inversion?
        Wait, I can use `edges: "both"` for G1 to handle both $pzp \rightarrow out$ and $pzn \rightarrow out$ if I arrange the switches differently? No, that's not how it works.

    *   Let's stick to `PSSHI_SyncHalf`. Let's double check the switch limit.
        S1, S2, S3 (3 switches). Limit is 4. Perfect.
        D1, D2, D3 (3 diodes). Limit is 16 components. Perfect.
